title: Early shift: Pellow & Finch
summary: Work the SOC desk for one shift: five alerts, most of them noise. Investigate the logs, decide what each one is, get other teams to act, and hand over to the next shift.
card: Five alerts, mostly noise. Find the real one
briefing: Morning. The night shift left you four alerts for Pellow & Finch, and more may come in. Most nights it's noise, but check each one properly: decide what it is, ask other teams to act where it's needed, and leave a clean handover. The clock only moves when you do something, so take your time reading.

clientImage.alt: Pellow & Finch's parcel depot: a warehouse with four loading bays, delivery vans and parcels in the yard

simplification: Simplified simulation: a real shift has more alerts and far longer logs. The Linux log lines follow Ubuntu 22.04's OpenSSH, sudo, shadow-utils (useradd, usermod, passwd) and nginx formats. The sign-in log is a generic SIEM export written for this shift: real identity providers and VPNs each have their own format. Countries are invented for the story, because documentation addresses have no real location. Department replies are scripted. All people and companies are fictional.

notes.name: Client notes: Pellow & Finch
notes.about: What Lanternfield knows about this client: systems, contacts and recent changes.
lines: Client: Pellow & Finch Logistics, parcel delivery, about 220 staff. Lanternfield monitors their servers, VPN and sign-ins.
Contact: Dana Whitfield, IT manager, 07:30 to 18:00. Report confirmed incidents to Dana.
web01: public parcel-tracking site (nginx on Ubuntu 22.04). Static pages and a tracking API. No WordPress, no PHP.
web01: SSH is open to the internet so the web admin, tbrooks, can log in from the office (198.51.100.23) with a key. Password logins are still enabled (CHG-2302 will switch them off).
files01: internal file server (Ubuntu 22.04), reachable only from the office and the VPN. IT support staff have sudo.
files01: server logins use directory names without the dot (m.okafor logs in as mokafor).
VPN: address pool 10.8.0.0/24. Full tunnel: while connected, staff internet traffic leaves through the VPN.
CHG-2291 (20 Oct): the VPN's internet exit moved from London (198.51.100.4) to the Amsterdam data centre (198.51.100.10). Staff on the VPN now appear to be in the Netherlands.
CHG-2240: MFA rollout for the VPN. Accounts not yet enrolled can still sign in with just a password until 31 Oct.
Network Ops block single addresses on request. Blocking anything wider needs a change ticket from the client.
Staff: j.patel (finance) works from home on Mondays and Wednesdays.
Staff: m.okafor (IT support) works 09:00 to 17:30.

findings.finding: Client change CHG-2291: since 20 Oct the VPN's internet exit is in Amsterdam (198.51.100.10), so staff on the VPN appear to be in the Netherlands.
Client change CHG-2240: VPN accounts not yet enrolled in MFA can still sign in with just a password until 31 Oct.
web01 runs no WordPress and no PHP, so probes for wp-login.php or phpunit can't succeed.
m.okafor works 09:00 to 17:30: 05:47 and 06:12 are well outside their hours.

alerts.title: Multiple failed SSH logins on web01
alerts.detection: web01: 9 failed SSH logins from 203.0.113.9 in 6 minutes (threshold: 5).

hints: Start in web01's auth.log. The question isn't whether someone tried, it's whether anything got in. Search for the address in the alert.
Every attempt from 203.0.113.9 says 'Failed password'. Now search 'Accepted' to see who did log in, and from where.
Only tbrooks's key from the office got in. Internet-facing SSH gets guessed at all the time: suspicious, but no harm done. Low severity, close it, no request needed.

evidence.text: auth.log: every attempt from 203.0.113.9 ended in 'Failed password'
evidence.why: Failures are the whole story here: the guesses didn't work.

evidence.text: auth.log: the only accepted logins were tbrooks's key from the office
evidence.why: This is what rules out harm: had a guess worked, there would be an 'Accepted password' line from 203.0.113.9.

evidence.text: auth.log: it tried usernames that don't exist (admin, ubuntu, pi)
evidence.why: Shows automated guessing from a list, which is what internet-facing SSH sees every day.

evidence.text: The alert fired, so someone must have got in
evidence.why: This alert counts failed logins: it says someone tried. Only an accepted login would show they got in.

summaries: Failed SSH logins on web01 overnight. Probably nothing.
SSH password guessing on web01 from 203.0.113.9 (9 attempts, 01:10 to 01:16). All failed; the only accepted logins were tbrooks's key from the office. No action needed.
Brute force on web01 from 203.0.113.9. The server may be compromised: recommend rebuilding web01.
answer.why: Internet-facing SSH gets guessed at constantly. What matters is whether a guess worked, and auth.log shows none did. Blocking one address is optional and does little, because the next scanner uses another. The lasting fix is already planned: CHG-2302 switches web01 to key-only logins.

alerts.title: Impossible travel: j.patel
alerts.detection: j.patel@pellowfinch.example signed in from GB (06:31) and then NL (06:48): 17 minutes apart, about 360 km.

hints: Impossible travel compares where public addresses are. Before suspecting j.patel, check the client notes for anything that changes where people appear to be.
Look at CHG-2291 in the notes, then j.patel's sign-ins: did a VPN connection come just before the 'NL' one? Do others on the VPN show the same address?
The VPN's internet exit moved to Amsterdam, and j.patel connected to the VPN at 06:44. It's legitimate: a false alarm. No action, and certainly no locking the account.

evidence.text: Client notes: the VPN's internet exit moved to Amsterdam (198.51.100.10) on 20 Oct
evidence.why: This explains the 'NL' location: it's the company's own VPN, not j.patel's position.

evidence.text: Sign-in log: j.patel connected to the VPN at 06:44, just before the 'NL' sign-in
evidence.why: Ties the jump to the VPN: once connected, j.patel's traffic left through Amsterdam.

evidence.text: Sign-in log: other staff on the VPN also appear from 198.51.100.10
evidence.why: If everyone on the VPN 'travels' to the Netherlands, it's the network, not the person.

evidence.text: Service Desk: j.patel confirmed both sign-ins were theirs
evidence.why: Direct confirmation from the user is good evidence, as long as it fits what the logs show.

evidence.text: j.patel's account was in the 05:46 password spray, so these sign-ins are suspect
evidence.why: That attempt failed. The later sign-ins came from j.patel's usual addresses and passed MFA.

summaries: False alarm: j.patel's 'NL' sign-in is the VPN's new Amsterdam exit (CHG-2291). j.patel connected to the VPN at 06:44 and passed MFA. Consider tuning the rule to ignore 198.51.100.10.
j.patel signed in from two countries. Account disabled as a precaution.
Possible account takeover of j.patel: they were also targeted by the VPN spray.
answer.why: Impossible-travel rules compare locations of public addresses, so a VPN or proxy makes people 'travel'. Here the client's own change calendar explains it, and the sign-ins passed MFA. Check before you escalate: disabling the account or worrying the client costs them real time.

alerts.title: Web server 404 spike on web01
alerts.detection: web01: 9 '404 Not Found' responses in one minute from one address (usual: under 2).

hints: A 404 spike usually means someone asking for pages that don't exist. Open web01's access.log and look at what 192.0.2.66 asked for, and the status codes it got.
/.env, /.git/config, /wp-login.php: a scanner hunting for common mistakes. Did any of those get a 200? The client notes say what web01 really runs.
Every probe got 404, and the home page 200 is just the public page. Real activity, no harm done: low severity, close it. Blocking one scanner is optional and won't stop the next.

evidence.text: access.log: every probe from 192.0.2.66 got 404 Not Found
evidence.why: Nothing the scanner asked for exists, so nothing was exposed.

evidence.text: access.log: well-known targets (/.env, /wp-login.php) asked for within seconds, by zgrab
evidence.why: Shows an automated scanner checking for common mistakes, not someone targeting this site.

evidence.text: Client notes: web01 runs no WordPress or PHP
evidence.why: Confirms the probes couldn't have worked even if a file had been there by accident.

evidence.text: access.log: 192.0.2.66 got a 200 for the home page, so it got in
evidence.why: The home page is public: anyone can load it. A 200 for /.env would have been a problem; a 200 for / is not.

summaries: Web attack on web01 from 192.0.2.66. Escalated to the client.
404 spike on web01. Couldn't tell what it was.
Automated scan of web01 from 192.0.2.66 (zgrab) at 06:41: 9 probes for common secret and admin paths, all 404. Only the public home page was served. No action needed.
answer.why: Every public web server is scanned many times a day. The questions are whether anything the scanner asked for existed, and whether anything other than public pages came back. Here, nothing did.

alerts.title: New account added to the sudo group on files01
alerts.detection: files01: user svcbackup2 added to privileged group 'sudo' (by mokafor via sudo).

hints: A new admin account is serious until proven otherwise. In files01's auth.log, search svcbackup2 to see who made it and when, then where that person logged in from.
mokafor logged in from 10.8.0.14, a VPN address; their usual one is 10.8.0.5. Open the impossible-travel alert's sign-in log and search 10.8.0.14 to see whose session that was.
That session came from the password spray (203.0.113.77): this is the attack, and it links to the spray alert. Lock svcbackup2, reset m.okafor (attach a finding when asked) and tell the client.

evidence.text: files01 auth.log: mokafor created svcbackup2, set its password and added it to sudo at 06:13 to 06:14
evidence.why: The change itself: a new account with full admin rights.

evidence.text: files01 auth.log: mokafor logged in at 06:12 from 10.8.0.14
evidence.why: Places the change in a session from a specific VPN address, which you can trace.

evidence.text: Sign-in log: 10.8.0.14 belonged to m.okafor's VPN session from the spraying address, 203.0.113.77
evidence.why: This is the link: the session that made the change came from the password spray, not from m.okafor.

evidence.text: Service Desk: m.okafor says they didn't do it
evidence.why: Supports the logs. On its own a denial proves little; with the logs, it's strong.

evidence.text: mokafor is in IT support and has sudo, so creating accounts is part of the job
evidence.why: Having the right to do something doesn't mean they did it. Out of hours, from a session that started with a spray, a new admin account is how attackers keep their access.

summaries: Attacker created svcbackup2 with sudo on files01 at 06:13, using m.okafor's account over a VPN session from the password spray (203.0.113.77). svcbackup2 locked, m.okafor reset, client informed. Check files01 for anything else changed since 06:12.
mokafor created a new account on files01. Probably IT support work; asked them to confirm.
files01 compromised. Recommend wiping all servers.
answer.why: A new admin account created out of hours is a classic way for an attacker to keep access. The logs alone show what happened; the sign-in log shows how. Lock the new account and end its session, reset the account that was used, and tell the client.

alerts.title: Password spray against the VPN
alerts.detection: VPN: 13 accounts tried from 203.0.113.77 between 05:41 and 05:47, 12 failed (raised by the hourly correlation rule).

hints: A spray tries one password on many accounts. In the sign-in log, search the address and check two things: how many accounts, and did any succeed?
m.okafor's sign-in from 203.0.113.77 at 05:47 succeeded, without MFA. Check the client notes for why that was still allowed, and look for what that session did next.
One account fell, and its VPN session made the files01 change: link this to the sudo alert. Block 203.0.113.77 (not the whole range), reset m.okafor and tell the client.

evidence.text: Sign-in log: 13 accounts tried from 203.0.113.77 in 6 minutes, once each
evidence.why: One password against many accounts, slowly, is a spray: it avoids lockouts that many guesses against one account would trigger.

evidence.text: Sign-in log: m.okafor signed in successfully from 203.0.113.77 at 05:47, without MFA
evidence.why: The spray worked. This turns noise into an incident.

evidence.text: Client notes: VPN logins without MFA are still allowed until 31 Oct
evidence.why: Explains why one guessed password was enough.

evidence.text: It all came from one address, so blocking it ends the problem
evidence.why: Blocking stops this address only. The attacker already has m.okafor's password and made their own admin account on files01.

summaries: Password spray on the VPN from 203.0.113.77. All attempts failed. Address blocked.

VPN password spray from 203.0.113.77 (05:41 to 05:47, 13 accounts) succeeded for m.okafor (no MFA). Linked to the new admin account on files01. Address blocked, m.okafor reset, client informed. Watch for sign-ins from other accounts without MFA.
Many failed VPN logins this morning; users should change their passwords.
answer.why: Most sprays fail and are noise. This one has a success in it, from an account without MFA, and the same session went on to make the files01 change. The alert arrived later than the harm it explains: that is normal, and why linking alerts matters.

requests.label: Lock svcbackup2 on files01 and end its sessions

replies.text: files01 is a production server, so we need a reason on the ticket before we lock accounts on it. Attach a finding and send it again.
Done. svcbackup2 is locked and its SSH session on files01 has been ended. We've kept the account, not deleted it, so its history can be investigated.

requests.label: Reset m.okafor's password and end their VPN sessions

replies.text: We need a reason on the ticket before we reset someone's password. Attach a finding and send it again.
Done. m.okafor's password is reset and their VPN session is ended. They'll have to enrol in MFA before they can sign in again.
We need a reason on the ticket before we disable someone's account. Attach a finding and send it again.
Done. j.patel's account is disabled. (Update: Pellow & Finch's finance team have called to ask why j.patel can't work.)
replies.cost: Disabled a legitimate user: j.patel was locked out of work for something the client's change calendar explained.

requests.label: Block 203.0.113.77 at the VPN gateway and edge firewall

replies.text: Done. 203.0.113.77 is blocked at the VPN gateway and the edge firewall.

requests.label: Block all of 203.0.113.0/24 at the edge

replies.text: We can't block a whole /24 without a change ticket from the client (it's in their notes). If you need the spraying address gone, ask us to block 203.0.113.77 and we'll do it now. For the wider range, ask the client contact to raise a ticket.
Done. Bear in mind SSH on web01 is open to the internet, so the next scanner will just come from a different address.
Done. It's a public website, though: scanners will keep coming from other addresses.

requests.label: Call j.patel to check this morning's sign-ins

replies.text: Spoke to j.patel: working from home today, connected to the VPN at about quarter to seven. Both sign-ins were theirs.

finding.finding: Service Desk: j.patel was working from home and connected to the VPN at about 06:45. Both sign-ins were theirs.

requests.label: Call m.okafor about this morning's activity

replies.text: Woke m.okafor up, sorry. They were asleep at 05:47 and haven't created any account. They admit their VPN password is one they've used on other sites.

finding.finding: Service Desk: m.okafor was asleep at 05:47 and didn't create any account. Their VPN password is reused on other sites.

requests.label: Report a confirmed incident: VPN account taken over, new admin account on files01

replies.text: Thanks for the clear report. I've told our MD, and we'll enforce MFA on the VPN for everyone today instead of waiting for 31 October. Send me the full timeline when you have it.

requests.label: Report j.patel's sign-ins from two countries as suspicious

replies.text: That'll be our VPN: we moved its internet exit to Amsterdam yesterday (CHG-2291), so everyone on it looks Dutch now. Worth checking our change calendar before escalating.
replies.cost: Escalated a false alarm to the client: the answer was in their own change calendar.

handover.links: Two alerts were one incident: the VPN session from the spray is the one that made the change. Linking alerts is how a SOC sees the whole attack.
handover.model: Overnight noise: SSH guessing on web01 (203.0.113.9) and a scan of web01 (192.0.2.66), both failed, no action. j.patel's impossible travel is the VPN's new Amsterdam exit (CHG-2291). Real incident: a password spray on the VPN from 203.0.113.77 (05:41 to 05:47) got m.okafor's password (no MFA). The attacker used that session to create svcbackup2 with sudo on files01 at 06:13. svcbackup2 locked, m.okafor reset, 203.0.113.77 blocked, Dana informed. Next shift: watch other accounts not enrolled in MFA, any sign-ins from 203.0.113.0/24, and check files01 for anything else changed since 06:12.
